strings.name: Félix Tshisekedi
strings.role: President of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and former rotating chair of the African Union
strings.summary: Félix Tshisekedi rose through the Union for Democracy and Social Progress, succeeding Joseph Kabila as president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2019 and beginning a second term in 2024. A former African Union chair, he has governed amid shifting domestic coalitions, eastern armed conflict, mineral cooperation and regional diplomacy. The fairness of both presidential elections was contested.
strings.coverageNote: Reviewed through 18 November 2026; recent activity includes his arrival in Cambodia on 14 November. The referendum law promulgated on 9 November sets procedures, rather than itself abolishing presidential term limits. Signing peace agreements does not establish that fighting has ended; implementation needs continued verification.
strings.influence.rationale: Since becoming president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, he has engaged with eastern security, mineral resources and regional diplomacy, influencing African governance.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and family background
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Kinshasa on 13 June 1963, he is the son of longtime opposition leader and former prime minister Étienne Tshisekedi. His father’s political career is distinct from his own subsequent presidential tenure.
strings.facts.f2.label: Early political path
strings.facts.f2.value: He spent part of his youth in exile with his family in Belgium and developed his political career within the Union for Democracy and Social Progress. Elected to a National Assembly seat for Mbuji-Mayi in 2011, he refused to take it in protest against the disputed election results.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Social policy and political competition
strings.highlights.h1.text: His government cites free primary education as an achievement, and he pledged jobs, better public services and security at his second inauguration. Opposition parties and observers criticised serious irregularities in the 2023 vote; the electoral commission said the problems did not affect the outcome. Policy promises and actual results require separate assessment.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Security, minerals and regional cooperation
strings.highlights.h2.text: The Washington framework with Rwanda links security commitments, regional economic integration and investment in mining and other sectors. Fighting continued in the east when it was signed. M23 did not participate in this bilateral signing; its Doha talks with the Congolese government followed a separate negotiating track.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Promulgating a new referendum law
strings.timeline.t1.text: He promulgated Law 26/045 setting procedures for referendums on a new constitution or existing constitutional provisions. Opponents feared it could pave the way for a third term. He denied seeking one but said he would accept if the people wanted it. Reporting on 11 November gave no referendum date; constitutional change was not already completed.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Signing the Washington joint declaration with Rwanda’s president
strings.timeline.t2.text: With Donald Trump witnessing, he and Paul Kagame reaffirmed implementation of the 27 June peace agreement and regional economic integration arrangements. The December declaration was not the original signing of the June agreement and did not establish that all security commitments had been fulfilled.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Taking the oath for a second presidential term
strings.timeline.t3.text: He was inaugurated at Kinshasa’s Martyrs Stadium for a second five-year term. The previous month’s election result was upheld through official procedures, but major opposition figures rejected it. The disputed electoral process is distinguished from the inauguration that took place.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Assuming the African Union’s rotating chairmanship
strings.timeline.t4.text: He succeeded South African President Cyril Ramaphosa in leading the AU’s heads-of-state-and-government work for 2021, handing over to Senegalese President Macky Sall on 5 February 2022. The rotating AU chair and African Union Commission chair are different positions.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Announcing the end of the coalition with Kabila’s camp
strings.timeline.t5.text: He ended the existing governing alliance and sought a new majority coalition in the National Assembly. His threat to dissolve parliament was conditional on failure to form a new majority, not an announcement that parliament had already been dissolved that day.
strings.timeline.t6.title: First presidential inauguration
strings.timeline.t6.text: Following the 30 December 2018 election, he succeeded Kabila in the first peaceful presidential handover since independence. The Constitutional Court rejected Martin Fayulu’s challenge, but counting disputes persisted. Tshisekedi’s and Kabila’s camps denied allegations of a private arrangement to manipulate the outcome.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Election as party leader and nomination for president
strings.timeline.t7.text: The Union for Democracy and Social Progress congress elected him leader and nominated him for president, continuing his father’s opposition tradition. Party nomination, the later national vote, announcement of results and inauguration were separate stages.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Winning a parliamentary seat but declining to take it
strings.timeline.t8.text: He won a National Assembly seat in Mbuji-Mayi, then refused to take it in response to his father’s call to boycott the election results. This should not be described as continuous parliamentary service beginning in 2011.
